speaker_role: former admissions director (former director of MBA admissions and financial aid at the Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania), now podcast host
commercial_incentive: No explicit service sale in this transcript, but hosts an admissions-advice podcast/social presence ('Admittedly') and repeatedly directs viewers to follow there; possible consultancy ties not stated directly in this episode.
key_insights: Argues test-optional policies were partly a deliberate marketing and yield tool: they widened applicant pools, let schools lower admit rates, and boosted perceived selectivity/rankings.

Claims colleges intentionally keep average test score bands lower than they technically could, to avoid discouraging strong applicants who are weak in just one section (e.g., a math-strong, verbal-weaker student).
Uses his own experience running Wharton MBA admissions (GMAT) to argue schools cap how many top scorers they admit so as not to discourage otherwise excellent applicants from applying at all.
Argues test-optional created a 'backdoor' letting schools admit development/athletic recruits without their lower scores showing up in reported class profile statistics.
Says submitted test scores have skewed upward because mainly high scorers choose to submit, making published Common Data Set ranges a less reliable benchmark now.
Predicts a broad shift back toward test-required policies, driven by grade inflation eroding trust in GPA and by legal/political pressure to demonstrate merit-based admissions.

Advises middle/upper-middle-class applicants from strong schools to submit scores, framing test-optional as realistically safest for first-gen/low-income students or applicants with truly unique circumstances.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker says at Wharton MBA admissions, of about 8,000-8,500 annual applications, over 3,000 had GMAT scores of 750+ (90th percentile or higher).
Speaker says middle-50% SAT bands at top schools usually run around 1520-1570.
Speaker names NYU, Columbia, and the University of California system as still test-optional/test-blind as of this recording.
notable_or_distinctive: Frames test-optional policy largely as a strategic/marketing and yield-management tool for colleges rather than a pure equity measure, including a 'backdoor' theory for hiding recruited-athlete or donor scores.
reliability_notes: Several claims (schools deliberately suppressing score averages, the 'backdoor' theory) are presented as insider insight but are unverified assertions rather than sourced data; policy specifics named here will need periodic re-checking as they change by year.
